stem: A media company keeps 1.2 billion click events in a Delta table. After feature encoding the training set is far larger than the memory of the biggest node type available, and a churn-style logistic regression must be retrained nightly on the full history. Scoring later runs on the same Spark cluster. Which training approach fits these constraints?

choices.text: Move the job to a single-node cluster and enlarge the swap space, so the whole training set can be paged in and fitted by scikit-learn
Train scikit-learn on a 0.1% random sample, because the rare customer segments in the business requirements are not needed for the model
Build a Spark ML `Pipeline` ending in `LogisticRegression` and fit it on the DataFrame so the rows stay partitioned across the workers
Call `toPandas()` on the full training DataFrame and fit scikit-learn `LogisticRegression` on the driver, using the largest driver type available

stem: A pricing team has a 3 GB table of features. Their best model so far is a scikit-learn `HistGradientBoostingRegressor` tuned by hand, and no Spark ML regressor has matched its error on this data. The team asks whether to rewrite training as a Spark ML pipeline "because the platform is Spark". What should the ML engineer recommend?

choices.text: Convert the model to a Spark ML `LinearRegression`, because linear models are the only family that can be trained on Spark clusters
Rewrite it as a Spark ML `GBTRegressor` on a 16-worker cluster, since distributed training is faster for tree ensembles
Keep scikit-learn but run `fit` inside a `mapInPandas` call so that the data is split over the workers and each worker trains a part of the model
Keep scikit-learn on a single-node cluster, prepare features in Spark and read them with `toPandas()`, and move to Spark ML if the data outgrows memory

stem: A Spark ML `RandomForestClassifier` is fitted on a 60 GB Delta table on a cluster with 10 workers of 16 cores. The Spark UI shows only 8 tasks in the training stages while 152 cores are idle, and the fit takes far longer than the team expected. The DataFrame was read from a table stored in 8 large files. What is the most effective change?

choices.text: Switch to scikit-learn on the driver, because Spark ML cannot use more cores than the number of input files in a Delta table
Repartition the training DataFrame to a small multiple of the total core count (for example 320) and cache it before calling `fit`
Raise `spark.driver.memory` so that the driver can hold the partitions that the 8 tasks are processing, which frees the other cores
Increase `numTrees` to 160 so that Spark ML creates one task per tree and fills the idle cores with work

stem: A 1 TB Delta table feeds a gradient-boosted tree model. A learning curve shows validation error flat once the training set exceeds roughly 2% of the rows (about 20 GB), and the team has a tuned XGBoost model for this problem. Spark ML training on the full table takes hours on a large cluster. Which plan is the best trade-off?

choices.text: Sample about 5% of the rows with Spark, train the tuned XGBoost model on a single large node, and re-check the curve when the data changes
Split the table by month and train 24 separate Spark ML models, then average their predictions, which makes each fit smaller
Add more workers to the Spark ML job until the full-data run takes minutes, and accept the higher cost because only the runtime was a concern
Train the Spark ML `GBTClassifier` on all 1 TB, since more rows can only improve the model and the cluster is already paid for

stem: After a scikit-learn `RandomForestClassifier(n_jobs=-1)` job moved from a single-node cluster to a cluster with one driver and 16 workers, the training time did not change at all and the worker CPU utilization stays near zero. What explains this?

choices.text: The Delta table was read with too few partitions, so the workers were never scheduled; repartitioning to 16 would spread the fit
`n_jobs=-1` limits scikit-learn to one process per Spark executor, and the executors must first be restarted
The workers are not attached to the notebook until `spark.conf.set("spark.ml.distributed", "true")` is set
scikit-learn runs in the Python process of the driver, so only the driver cores are used and the workers have no part of the fit

stem: A team compares two prototypes on a 5 GB table: scikit-learn on a single-node cluster trains in 40 seconds, while the same algorithm in Spark ML on 10 workers takes 6 minutes. Management asks whether Spark ML is just configured badly. Which explanation is most accurate?

choices.text: For data that fits in memory, fixed costs of distributed training (task scheduling, shuffles, network aggregation) can dominate, so one node is faster
The result shows that the 10 workers are too small, and doubling the cluster would bring Spark ML below the single-node time at this data size
Spark ML uses only the driver for tree algorithms, so adding workers cannot reduce the runtime at any data size
Spark ML always reads the data twice as often as scikit-learn, so it is expected to be slower at every data size and cluster size

stem: A 200-million-row churn table has nulls in `income` and `tenure_months`. The `VectorAssembler` stage fails on them, and the first fix, filtering the null rows before training, would also drop a large share of new customers. Scoring batches contain nulls as well. How should the pipeline be changed?

choices.text: Fill the nulls with `df.fillna(0)` in the training notebook, then repeat the same call in each scoring job
Add an `Imputer(strategy="median")` stage before `VectorAssembler`, so medians learned at `fit` are stored in the model
Compute the mean of each column with `agg` on the training table and write it into a SQL expression in every consumer
Set the `VectorAssembler` option `handleInvalid` to skip, then accept that scoring batches return fewer rows than were sent in and rejoin them

stem: The feature `ctr = clicks / impressions` is added with `df.withColumn("ctr", ...)` in the training notebook, and the logistic regression pipeline is fitted on the result. The scoring team receives the saved `PipelineModel` and finds the model fails because `ctr` is missing from the raw tables. How should the training code be changed so the logic travels with the model?

choices.text: Write `ctr` to the raw table in a nightly job for all consumers
Document the formula in the model description so that each consuming team can add the column before scoring
Add a first `SQLTransformer` stage (`SELECT *, clicks / impressions AS ctr FROM __THIS__`) so the model computes it
Create a Python UDF in the scoring job that computes `ctr`, and register it under the same name as the column

stem: A text pipeline produces TF-IDF vectors with 8 million dimensions, stored as sparse vectors of about 150 non-zero values each. Linear models on them need features on a comparable scale, and a trial with `StandardScaler(withMean=True)` ran out of executor memory. Which stage keeps the vectors sparse and still rescales the features?

choices.text: `StandardScaler(withMean=True)` with a higher executor memory setting, since centering is needed for every linear model
`MinMaxScaler`, because mapping each feature to the range 0 to 1 leaves all the zeros in place
`RobustScaler(withCentering=True)`, because removing the median is cheaper than removing the mean
`MaxAbsScaler`, which divides each feature by its largest absolute value and does not center the data

stem: A pipeline for a streaming source has stages `[VectorAssembler(inputCols=["emb", "amount"]), classifier]`, where `emb` is a `VectorUDT` column produced by an upstream step. Fitting on historical batch data works, but starting the query that applies the `PipelineModel` to the streaming DataFrame fails because the size of `emb` is unknown. Which stage solves this?

choices.text: A `VectorSizeHint(inputCol="emb", size=64)` stage placed before the `VectorAssembler`
A `VectorSlicer` on `emb` with the indices 0 to 63, which fixes the size by selecting a subset of values
A `Normalizer` on `emb`, because normalizing a vector also writes the vector length into the column metadata
A `.cache()` call on the streaming DataFrame, so that Spark can look at the contents of `emb` and infer the vector size

stem: Several models (churn, upsell, support risk) share one featurization: indexing four categorical columns, one-hot encoding them, and assembling a vector. The team wants one reusable, fitted artifact for the shared featurization and separate model stages per use case. Which design applies Spark ML correctly?

choices.text: Fit the shared stages once with `fit` and call `collect()` on the result, then rebuild a `Pipeline` per model from the collected rows
Build a featurization `Pipeline` and use it as the first stage of each model `Pipeline`, since a `Pipeline` is itself an `Estimator`
Replace the shared stages by a `PipelineModel` object in the stage list of each model pipeline after calling `fit`
Create three copies of the same stage objects and put one copy into each `Pipeline`, because a stage instance may be used in only one pipeline

stem: A weekly job refits a whole `Pipeline` (`StringIndexer` on `merchant_category`, then a model) and also writes the indexed column to a Delta feature table that other teams read. After a refit, an older downstream model started producing wrong predictions, although the indexer code did not change. What is the most robust fix?

choices.text: Increase `maxCategories` on the indexer so that it learns every category and keeps the old indices stable
Refit the indexer on 10% of the data, because indices only depend on the sample size, not on the content
Store the raw category in the shared table and apply each model's own fitted `PipelineModel` at read time, so the mapping matches
Set `stringOrderType="alphabetAsc"` on the indexer, which keeps indices identical across refits even when new categories appear in the data

stem: A support-ticket model must predict the priority labels "low", "medium" and "high" stored as strings. Fitting a `LogisticRegression` on the string label column fails, and downstream reports need the original strings in the prediction output. Which stages solve both needs?

choices.text: A `Bucketizer` with splits at 1 and 2 on the label column, then a Python dictionary applied in the reporting job for the strings and a manual check
A `cast("int")` on the label column, and a stored lookup table maintained by hand for the report
A `StringIndexer` on the label, then an `IndexToString` stage after the classifier that maps `prediction` back
A `OneHotEncoder` on the label column, then reading the largest element of its vector as the prediction

stem: A feature `age` must become five bins. The business wants bins with roughly equal numbers of customers in the training data, learned once and reused unchanged when scoring later batches. Which stage fits?

choices.text: `Binarizer` applied five times with different thresholds, each producing one bin indicator
`QuantileDiscretizer(numBuckets=5)`, which learns quantile splits and returns a fixed `Bucketizer`
`StandardScaler`, because z-scores split in the same way as quantiles
`Bucketizer` with splits computed again on each scoring batch, so the bins always follow the current customer population

stem: A text classifier uses `Tokenizer`, then either `HashingTF` or `CountVectorizer`, then `IDF`, then logistic regression. Reviewers require a report of the ten words with the largest positive weights for each class, and the corpus has several million distinct terms. Which choice satisfies the requirement?

choices.text: `CountVectorizer` with a limited `vocabSize` and `minDF`, because its fitted model stores the vocabulary so that coefficient positions map back to words
`HashingTF` with `numFeatures` of 2^10, because the hashing trick keeps the vocabulary and gives each word a readable name
`HashingTF` with a very large `numFeatures`, because with enough buckets the hash index can be inverted to the word with no extra information
Neither; `IDF` already keeps the term names, so either vectorizer works and the report can be produced from the `IDF` model

stem: A team tunes a Spark ML `ALS` recommender with `CrossValidator` and `RegressionEvaluator(metricName="rmse")`. Every candidate returns an RMSE of `NaN`, so no best model can be chosen. Validation folds contain users and items that never appeared in the training folds. What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Increase `rank` to 200 so that the factors cover the unseen users and items
Set `nonnegative=True` on `ALS`, which constrains factors and so prevents NaN predictions for unknown users and items
Switch the evaluator to `mae`, which ignores NaN predictions
Set `coldStartStrategy="drop"` on `ALS`, so NaN prediction rows are removed before the metric is computed

stem: A marketing team clusters customers with Spark ML `KMeans` on `annual_income` (range 20,000 to 400,000) and `visits_per_month` (range 0 to 30). The clusters turn out to be almost only income bands. What change addresses the cause?

choices.text: Replace `KMeans` with `LogisticRegression`, which handles features on different scales and groups customers automatically
Raise `maxIter` to 500 so that the algorithm eventually weights the visit counts
Add a `StandardScaler` stage on the assembled vector before `KMeans`, so both features contribute comparably to distances
Increase `k` until the visit counts start to split the clusters

stem: A genomics model uses 8,000 continuous features and a categorical label with 4 classes. The team wants a Spark ML stage that keeps the 200 features most associated with the label before training a random forest. Which stage and settings apply?

choices.text: `PCA` with `k=200`, since principal components are the 200 original features with the highest scores
`UnivariateFeatureSelector` with `featureType="continuous"`, `labelType="categorical"` (ANOVA F-test) and `numTopFeatures` selection of 200
`ChiSqSelector`, because the features are continuous and it computes a correlation between each feature and the label before the forest
`VarianceThresholdSelector` with the label column as input, which keeps the features that vary most with the label

stem: A fraud model is tuned with `CrossValidator(numFolds=5)`. Each customer has many transactions, and cross-validation scores are far higher than the scores on later customers. The team suspects the folds. What change is the best fix?

choices.text: Add a fold column such as `abs(hash(customer_id)) % 5` and pass it with `setFoldCol("fold")`
Set the seed of the `CrossValidator` so the same random folds are used for every parameter combination and run
Switch to `TrainValidationSplit(trainRatio=0.8)`, which splits at random and so avoids sharing customers
Raise `numFolds` to 20 so that each validation fold is smaller

stem: A `CrossValidator` runs a random forest grid on 4 workers of 16 cores each. A single forest fit on the 400 GB training set already keeps all executors busy. An engineer sets `setParallelism(24)` to finish faster, but the run is no quicker and some stages fail with executor memory errors. What is the best explanation and action?

choices.text: Parallelism above 1 is not allowed for tree algorithms, which is why executors fail; set it back to 1
Parallelism only affects the validation step, so the memory errors come from a bad grid and the setting can stay at 24
Parallelism must be at least the number of workers times cores (64), because lower values leave tasks unscheduled
Parallelism fits several settings at once, so concurrent fits compete for executors and memory; use a small value

stem: A team wants to pick `k` for a Spark ML `KMeans` model on 80 million unlabeled customers. They build a `ParamGridBuilder` over `k` from 3 to 12 and need an evaluator for `TrainValidationSplit`, which picks the best `ParamMap` by the evaluator metric. There is no label column. Which evaluator fits?

choices.text: `MulticlassClassificationEvaluator(metricName="f1")`, comparing the cluster index with a column of random labels
`RegressionEvaluator(metricName="rmse")` on the cluster index, since lower distance to the centre is the better fit
`BinaryClassificationEvaluator`, because each cluster is a positive class against all of the others
`ClusteringEvaluator`, which computes the silhouette score from the `features` and `prediction` columns and needs no label

stem: A gradient-boosted model has six hyperparameters with continuous ranges. A full grid would need over 15,000 combinations, and the team wants to try 40 random combinations with Spark MLlib cross-validation. Which approach works?

choices.text: Set `numFolds=40` so that `CrossValidator` evaluates 40 random subsets of the grid
Pass a `scipy` distribution object to `addGrid` for each parameter, and `CrossValidator` will then draw 40 random samples from them
Sample 40 combinations in Python, build one `ParamMap` per combination into a list, and pass the list to `setEstimatorParamMaps`
Use `ParamGridBuilder().setRandom(40)` before `build()`, which makes the builder sample the grid

stem: A demand-forecasting pipeline is tuned with `CrossValidator` on two years of daily rows. The cross-validated RMSE is excellent, but after deployment the error on the following month is twice as high. Folds were created at random. What is the most likely cause and the right change?

choices.text: The grid was too small; add more parameter combinations and keep the random folds
Random folds mix past and future days, so models train on later days; split by time and validate on a later period
The data was not shuffled before cross-validation; shuffle it again and increase `numFolds` to get a stable estimate
The evaluator is wrong; `RegressionEvaluator` cannot be used on time-ordered data

stem: A team tunes a `Pipeline` with `CrossValidator` and logs `max(cvModel.avgMetrics)` of 0.91 AUC in the model card as the expected production quality. A reviewer objects. Which practice is correct?

choices.text: Hold out a test set that is never used in tuning, evaluate `cvModel.bestModel` on it once, and report that score
Keep the maximum; the best parameter map was chosen on validation data, so its score is unbiased and can be reported
Refit the best model on the whole data and report its score on the training data, which is the largest sample
Log the average of `avgMetrics` instead of the maximum, because the maximum includes the best fold

stem: A team launches 40 parallel Optuna workers on Spark, but each worker builds its own study with the default in-memory storage, as in `study = optuna.create_study()`. Every worker reports a different "best" result, and TPE never learns from the trials of other workers. Which change fixes the design?

choices.text: Create the study with `MlflowStorage` for the experiment and run it through `MlflowSparkStudy`, so all workers share one study
Make every worker use `RandomSampler` with the same seed, so that all in-memory studies visit the same points in order
Collect each worker's study on the driver after the run and merge the trial lists into one summary table by hand
Raise the number of trials on each worker so that every in-memory study collects enough history to find the same optimum

stem: A team compares its Optuna setup with an older Hyperopt job. It calls `MlflowSparkStudy(study_name="gbt", storage=storage)` without passing a sampler or pruner. Which algorithms does the study use by default?

choices.text: A grid sampler over the first suggested values and a successive-halving pruner that stops half of the trials
A random-search sampler with no early stopping, so the study behaves like a fixed grid until a pruner is set
The CMA-ES sampler for continuous spaces and a hyperband pruner that allocates resources to promising trials
`TPESampler` to propose new parameters and `MedianPruner` to stop trials that look worse than the median

stem: A team runs a notebook on an older cluster runtime, and `from mlflow.pyspark.optuna.study import MlflowSparkStudy` raises an import error. The same notebook works on the team's newer runtime, which already includes MLflow 3. What is the best fix on the older cluster?

choices.text: Import only `MlflowStorage` and pass it to a plain `optuna.create_study`, because that class exists in every MLflow version and Spark needs no study wrapper
Run `%pip install mlflow --upgrade` and `%pip install optuna` first in the notebook, or use a runtime with MLflow 3
Replace the import with `hyperopt.SparkTrials`, which is the maintained way to run Optuna objectives on executors
Copy the MLflow 3 package folder from the newer cluster into the old one so that the Spark executors find the same classes

stem: A team tunes a neural network for 50 epochs per trial with `MlflowSparkStudy` and the default pruner. Poor trials still run all 50 epochs, and the log shows no pruned trials. The objective only trains the model and returns the final validation loss. What should the engineer change?

choices.text: Raise `n_jobs` so that Spark can interrupt long trials from outside the executor task once enough of them run in parallel
Raise `n_trials` above 100, because the default pruner stays inactive until it has seen a hundred completed trials in the study
Make the objective report its validation loss to the trial after every epoch and stop the trial when the pruner marks it as unpromising
Switch the storage backend from `MlflowStorage` to a local SQLite file on the driver, because MLflow storage disables every pruner in the study

stem: A team ports a Hyperopt job that used `hp.loguniform("C", np.log(1e-10), np.log(1e10))` and `SparkTrials(parallelism=20)` to Optuna on Databricks. Which port matches the pattern in the Databricks Optuna example?

choices.text: `trial.suggest_categorical("C", [1e-10, 1e-5, 1, 1e5, 1e10])` declared before the objective, with `MlflowSparkStudy` acting as the sampler
`trial.suggest_float("C", 1e-10, 1e10)` on the default linear scale, because Optuna rescales very wide ranges to a log scale automatically
`trial.suggest_float("C", 1e-10, 1e10, log=True)` inside the objective, with the study run by `MlflowSparkStudy` on a shared `MlflowStorage`
`trial.suggest_float("C", np.log(1e-10), np.log(1e10))` in the objective, with `SparkTrials(parallelism=20)` passed to `optuna.create_study`

stem: A study runs several hundred concurrent trials on Spark. Each trial reports its parameters and metrics to the MLflow tracking server, and the team sees throttled REST calls and slow trials. A colleague proposes dropping `MlflowStorage` in favor of a custom `mlflow.log_param` call in each objective. Why is `MlflowStorage` the better design?

choices.text: It samples a subset of the trials and logs only those, which keeps the number of REST calls roughly constant
It caches all trial results in driver memory and writes a single batch after the last trial, so no REST call happens during the search
It replaces the MLflow tracking server by a Delta table, so REST calls to the tracking server are never made at all
It batches writes and flushes them on an interval or at a size threshold, which avoids throttling of the tracking REST API

stem: A data scientist runs `setup_ray_cluster(max_worker_nodes=4)` in a notebook that is attached to serverless compute, and the call fails. The goal is to run Ray Tune for CPU-based models. Which option does the Databricks documentation support?

choices.text: Add `autoscale=True` to the call, because serverless compute only needs the autoscaling flag for the Ray-on-Spark integration
Attach the notebook to a dedicated (single user) or no-isolation shared ML cluster, or to a jobs cluster, and create the Ray cluster there
Switch the notebook to standard (shared) access mode, which runs each Ray worker in an isolated container with full Ray support
Install `ray[default]` with `%pip` in the serverless session so that the Ray head process is started inside the serverless sandbox

stem: A nightly job tunes models with Ray Tune. Several analysts also want to submit Ray tasks to the same Ray cluster during the day through `ray.init()` from their own notebooks. A cluster created with `setup_ray_cluster` in the first analyst's notebook disappears whenever that notebook detaches. Which setup fits?

choices.text: Start a global mode Ray cluster with `setup_global_ray_cluster` from a notebook job, and let users connect with `ray.init()`
Run `setup_ray_cluster` in every analyst's notebook with the same arguments, so that all of them share the first cluster's workers
Run the Ray head on a laptop and connect the Databricks workers to it with the Ray Job CLI and `ray start`
Use `setup_ray_cluster` and raise the idle timeout so the cluster stays alive after the notebook detaches

stem: A team has a running Ray cluster that executes a long Ray Tune search. A data scientist runs `%pip install lightgbm` in the same notebook to add a library for a new experiment, and the whole Ray cluster stops. What is the documented way to avoid this?

choices.text: Run `%pip install` from a second notebook, because only the notebook that created the Ray cluster is affected by pip
Install the library with `%pip` on every Ray worker through a Ray remote function that calls `subprocess` at the start of each trial
Install libraries before the Ray cluster is created, either at the top of the notebook or as cluster libraries
Call `ray.shutdown()` before `%pip` and `ray.init()` afterwards, because pip always needs the Ray client to be disconnected first

stem: A Ray Tune job on Databricks reports each trial to MLflow, but the trials fail with credential errors inside the Ray tasks, while MLflow logging works in the notebook itself. Which step does the documentation require for MLflow with Ray Tune, Ray Train or custom Ray tasks?

choices.text: Run the Tune job from the Ray head node only, since remote Ray tasks are never allowed to call the MLflow tracking server
Pass the notebook's access token as an argument to every `tune.report` call so that each worker authenticates when it reports, and rotate it per trial
Call `mlflow.autolog()` once on the driver, which carries the notebook's credentials to every Ray worker automatically
Set `DATABRICKS_HOST` and a token (or client ID and secret) as environment variables before `setup_ray_cluster`

stem: A fixed-size Databricks cluster of 10 workers runs a Spark feature job for two hours and then a Ray Tune search for two hours. A Ray cluster created with a fixed `max_worker_nodes=10` keeps all workers busy as Ray nodes, so the Spark stage queues behind it. How should the team configure the hybrid workload?

choices.text: Enable Ray-on-Spark autoscaling with minimum and maximum worker nodes, and keep `spark.executor.memory` small, so idle Ray workers are freed
Raise `spark.executor.memory` as high as possible so that Spark caches more data and finishes before Ray starts
Reduce the Ray cluster to a single worker for the whole day, because Ray and Spark cannot share a cluster at all
Start one global Ray cluster for each Spark task with `setup_global_ray_cluster`, so that every Spark job owns its own Ray head and workers

stem: A team preprocesses data with Spark and then trains with Ray Tune on a GPU cluster. Spark preprocessing tasks sometimes grab GPUs, which leaves fewer GPUs for Ray, and the CPU-only Spark stages have fewer task slots than the instance has cores. Which cluster setting does Databricks recommend?

choices.text: Set `num_cpus_head_node` and `num_gpus_head_node` to zero so the Ray head cannot take any resources from Spark
Set the Spark cluster configuration `spark.task.resource.gpu.amount` to `0` so Spark transformations do not claim GPUs
Set `spark.task.resource.gpu.amount` to the number of GPUs per node so each Spark task owns all of the node's GPUs
Set `spark.executor.memory` to the full node memory so that Spark never competes for resources with the Ray object store

stem: A team trains a PyTorch network that fits easily in the memory of one GPU, on a dataset that also fits on one machine. A colleague proposes an 8-node GPU cluster with distributed training "to be faster". What does Databricks guidance recommend?

choices.text: Use a CPU cluster of 8 nodes, since GPU instances cannot be combined with distributed training libraries in Databricks Runtime ML
Always distribute neural network training, because communication overhead is smaller than the compute gained on every dataset size and model
Convert the network to a Spark ML pipeline, because Spark ML models scale better than neural networks on a single node
Train on one machine, moving to a larger or multi-GPU instance if needed, and distribute only when model or data exceed memory

stem: A data scientist develops in a local IDE through Databricks Connect against Standard compute on Databricks Runtime 17.0 or above. The training DataFrame is far too large for the laptop, and the model is a classical Spark ML algorithm. The team wants distributed training without managing a dedicated ML cluster. What does Databricks offer?

choices.text: `TorchDistributor` launched from the IDE, because it is the module Databricks documents for training Spark ML models on Standard compute
The `pyspark.ml.connect` module, which Databricks documents for distributed training and inference of Spark ML models on Standard compute
A `toPandas()` call in the IDE session followed by a scikit-learn fit, since the Databricks Connect client sends the fit to the cluster
A global Ray cluster started from the IDE with `setup_global_ray_cluster`, because Standard compute supports Ray only for Spark ML algorithms

stem: A multi-node GPU training job on four nodes fails at start-up with `ncclInternalError: Internal check failed`, although the same code runs on one node. The message points to a problem with network communication among the GPUs. Which fix does the Databricks documentation give?

choices.text: Change the backend from `nccl` to `gloo` on the GPU nodes, because gloo is the documented replacement for NCCL on multi-node GPU clusters
Set `NCCL_P2P_DISABLE` to `1` in the training code, because it forces NCCL to use the primary network interface between nodes
Add `os.environ["NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME"] = "eth0"` to the training code so that NCCL uses the primary network interface
Double `num_processes` beyond the GPU count, so that NCCL opens more sockets and can pick a working network interface

stem: A team distributes PyTorch training over 8 GPU nodes and measures a 6x speed-up compared with 1 node. Doubling to 16 nodes gives only 1.2x more. GPU utilization on each node drops during the steps. What is the most likely cause and the right reaction?

choices.text: Synchronization overhead grows with nodes; use fewer, larger machines or more GPUs per node if the model fits
Spark is limiting the number of tasks; set `spark.task.resource.gpu.amount` to `0` to give the extra nodes more work in each step
The model is too small for a GPU; replace the GPUs with a CPU cluster of 32 nodes to restore the speed-up
The cluster autoscaled down during training; enable autoscaling so that Spark removes idle GPU nodes mid-run

stem: A cluster has 6 worker nodes, each with 4 GPUs and 48 cores. A team runs `setup_ray_cluster(max_worker_nodes=6)` and starts Ray Tune trials that each request one GPU. The trials never start, although the GPUs of the cluster are idle. What should the engineer change?

choices.text: Pass `num_cpus_worker_node=48` and `num_gpus_worker_node=4`, so that each Spark worker hosts one Ray worker owning all of its cores and GPUs
Set `num_gpus_head_node=4`, because the Ray head schedules every GPU trial and hands out the GPUs of the workers to the trials
Set `spark.executor.memory` to a small value such as 4g, because Spark executors keep all GPUs reserved until their memory is reduced
Raise `max_worker_nodes` to 24, one for each GPU in the cluster, because the number of Ray workers decides how many GPUs Ray can see

stem: A forecasting team currently fits a scikit-learn model on one large memory-optimized node. Data doubles each year. The team asks for the strongest argument for investing in a distributed Spark ML implementation now, although today's job runs fine on one node. Which argument is correct?

choices.text: Spark ML models require no additional validation, because partitioned data removes the risk of overfitting
Single-node training cannot be tracked in MLflow, so only distributed jobs can be logged to the experiment
Vertical scaling stops at the largest node, whereas data-parallel training grows by adding workers, at the price of communication overhead
Distributed training is always faster than single-node training for every data size, so the job will speed up immediately and cost less

stem: A vision team has a model that fits in the memory of one GPU, but the 4 TB image dataset takes days to cover per epoch on one GPU. The team has a cluster of GPU nodes and wants faster epochs. Which parallelization strategy fits?

choices.text: Vertical scaling of the driver node only, because PyTorch reads images on the driver and trains on the workers
Data parallelism with `TorchDistributor`: each process holds a full model copy, reads its own data shard and syncs gradients
Model parallelism, where each GPU holds a different layer block and the batch moves through them as a pipeline
Hyperparameter parallelism, where each GPU trains the same model on the same full dataset with another learning rate and a different seed

stem: A team wants to fine-tune a language model whose weights and optimizer state do not fit in the memory of a single GPU. Plain data-parallel replicas run out of GPU memory immediately. Which Databricks option is recommended for models that need higher compute but are limited by memory?

choices.text: A larger `TorchDistributor` with `num_processes` doubled, so that each GPU holds half of a complete model replica
Ray Tune, which splits a model across GPUs when a trial reports that the memory of one GPU is full
Spark ML `pyspark.ml` estimators, which shard neural network weights across executors automatically when the DataFrame is large and wide
The DeepSpeed distributor, built on TorchDistributor, with optimized memory use and pipeline parallelism

stem: A notebook launches `TorchDistributor(num_processes=4, local_mode=False, use_gpu=True).run(train, 1e-3)`. The job fails with errors that objects cannot be found or pickled on the executors. The `train` function imports `torch` at the top of the notebook and calls helper functions that use `torch` too. What is the documented fix?

choices.text: Set `local_mode=True`, which removes the need to ship any function from the driver to the executors
Convert the function to a lambda expression because pickle cannot serialize named functions
Wrap the call in `spark.sparkContext.broadcast(torch)`, so the imported module object is available on every executor and in every task
Put the import statements, such as `import torch`, inside the training function and inside any other function it calls

stem: A team moves single-GPU code to 4 processes with `TorchDistributor`. The model is wrapped in `DistributedDataParallel`, but the data loader is still `DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=64)`. Epoch time barely improves, and each process sees every sample. What should be changed?

choices.text: Pass `sampler=DistributedSampler(dataset)` to the `DataLoader`, so each process reads a distinct shard of every epoch
Increase `batch_size` to the size of the whole dataset, so that every process finishes in one step
Replace DDP with `DataParallel` on the driver, which assigns different rows to each worker automatically
Set `spark.task.resource.gpu.amount` to `0`, because Spark tasks otherwise read the data twice on each GPU of a node

stem: A team has 64 GPUs. Each tuning trial of its model trains with data parallelism over 8 GPUs, and there are 40 trials to run. The team wants the search to finish as fast as possible with this budget. Which plan is best?

choices.text: Run the 40 trials one at a time on all 64 GPUs, since a single distributed fit always has the highest total throughput
Run about 8 trials at a time, each on its own 8 GPUs, rather than every trial on all 64 GPUs in sequence
Run all 40 trials at once on 64 GPUs by giving each trial 1.6 GPUs through fractional sharing
Run each trial on a single GPU and skip data parallelism, because trial-level parallelism always beats data parallelism

stem: A team trains a gradient-boosted classifier and a logistic regression on a 2 TB Delta table of tabular features. The data cannot fit on one node. The team asks whether to use `TorchDistributor` for the distributed training. Which answer is correct?

choices.text: No, tabular data cannot be trained in a distributed way at all, so the table must be sampled down to fit on one machine
Yes, but only with `local_mode=True`, which spreads the 2 TB across all workers automatically
No, use Spark ML estimators, which parallelize over DataFrame partitions, and keep TorchDistributor for PyTorch code
Yes, since TorchDistributor distributes any scikit-learn estimator after you wrap it in a PyTorch module

stem: A churn model trains on `ml.crm.customer_features`, a table with one row per `customer_id` that a nightly job overwrites in place. Labels span the last 12 months and carry `churn_event_ts`. Offline AUC is 0.97, but the endpoint reaches only 0.71. What is the right repair?

choices.text: Add `lookback_window=timedelta(days=7)` to the existing `FeatureLookup` so that feature values older than a week are excluded from the joined training set
Keep every nightly row in a time series feature table keyed `(customer_id, ts TIMESERIES)` and pass `timestamp_lookup_key="churn_event_ts"` in the `FeatureLookup`
Raise the number of cross-validation folds and stratify by the churn label so that the rows whose features leak the outcome are spread evenly across folds
Repartition the label DataFrame by `customer_id` before `create_training_set` so each label is joined to the feature row computed on its own executor

stem: A fraud model was trained with `FeatureLookup(table_name="ml.risk.acct_features", feature_names=["spend_30d"], lookup_key="acct_id", timestamp_lookup_key="txn_ts", lookback_window=timedelta(days=7))`. In training, accounts with no feature row in the prior 7 days got `null`. In production, the endpoint returns 40-day-old `spend_30d` for dormant accounts and scores shift. What explains this and what should the team do?

choices.text: The window applies to training and batch scoring only; online lookups always return the latest value, so the team must flag stale values itself, e.g. with a last-updated feature
The online store retains every historical row, so add the current date to the lookup key and make the application pass today's date with each request
The endpoint enforces the window when a request carries a `txn_ts` field, so add the transaction time to each scoring request
The window is enforced online once the online table is republished in `SNAPSHOT` mode, so schedule a nightly snapshot publish to apply the limit

stem: A time series feature table `ml.iot.room_features` has key `(room, ts TIMESERIES)` and features `temp`, `co2`, `light`. A temperature job writes rows with only `room`, `ts` and `temp`. Training sets now show `null` for `co2` on many rows although a valid `co2` row exists a few minutes earlier. What is the cause and the fix?

choices.text: As-of lookup skips null cells only when `lookback_window` is set, so set a one-day window on the `FeatureLookup` and the earlier `co2` value is selected again
`write_table` in merge mode cannot target a time series feature table, so switch the job to overwrite so that nulls are replaced with the last known readings
As-of lookup takes the latest row at or before the label time and keeps its nulls, so write complete rows with every feature per timestamp
Features are joined per column, so list `co2` as a separate primary key column and the join then falls back to an earlier timestamp

stem: A model was trained from a time series feature table using `FeatureLookup(..., lookup_key="cust_id", timestamp_lookup_key="order_ts")`, and logged with `fe.log_model`. The nightly batch DataFrame has `cust_id` and `order_date` (a `DATE` column). What must the DataFrame passed to `fe.score_batch` contain?

choices.text: `cust_id` and any `DATE` or `TIMESTAMP` column, because `score_batch` finds the time column by type and casts it as needed
`cust_id` plus the feature table's own `ts` column, because the batch rows must carry the timeseries key of the stored table
Only `cust_id`, because `score_batch` uses the time of the scoring job as the as-of time for every row that it looks up
`cust_id` and a timestamp column named `order_ts` with the same data type used when the training set was created

stem: A time series feature table with 8 billion rows is joined to 200 million labels through `create_training_set`. Training-set builds are slow. The table has primary key `(user_id, ts TIMESERIES)`. Which change best speeds up the point-in-time joins without changing results?

choices.text: Partition the table by date and by `user_id` so that every as-of lookup scans a single small partition for its timestamp
Add `hour` and `minute` columns to the primary key so that each lookup matches a narrower key before the timestamp comparison
Enable liquid clustering on the table, use a current `databricks-feature-engineering`, and pass `use_spark_native_join=True` on Photon-enabled compute
Declare the table as a regular feature table keyed `(user_id, ts)` as strings so that lookups become exact matches that are simpler to execute

stem: A reviewer suggests dropping time series feature tables: "read the single-row feature table with `VERSION AS OF` at each label's date and union the results." Why is Delta time travel not a replacement for a point-in-time join in a feature store?

choices.text: Time travel reads the whole table at one commit per query, while an as-of join picks the latest row per key for each label, and time travel depends on log retention
Time travel and as-of joins are the same operation, so the union of versions gives identical results, only slower because every version is read separately
Time travel cannot read tables that have a primary key constraint, so feature tables are excluded from older-version reads and only plain tables qualify
Time travel returns data only for the 30 most recent commits, which is shorter than any labeling period, whereas as-of joins keep every historical row

stem: `ml.sales.store_stats` is an existing Delta table with no constraints, owned by the analyst. Its `store_id` and `snap_ts TIMESTAMP` columns are nullable and hold 14 months of hourly history. It must become a point-in-time feature table in place, without copying the data. Which sequence works?

choices.text: Run `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT store_stats_pk PRIMARY KEY (store_id, snap_ts TIMESERIES)` directly, because Unity Catalog sets key columns to NOT NULL while it adds the constraint
Run `ALTER COLUMN ... SET NOT NULL` on both key columns, then `ADD CONSTRAINT ... PRIMARY KEY (store_id, snap_ts TIMESERIES)`, which makes it a time series feature table
Add `PRIMARY KEY (store_id, snap_ts)` after setting both columns to NOT NULL, then pass `timeseries_columns="snap_ts"` in every `FeatureLookup` so that the lookups run as of the label time
Create a new table with `CREATE TABLE AS SELECT` that declares the key and `TIMESERIES` in its DDL, because a primary key can only be declared when a table is first created

stem: A feature job keeps daily history in `ml.crm.cust_daily` with primary key `(cust_id, snap_date DATE)`. The key was created without the `TIMESERIES` keyword, and `create_training_set` now raises an error about the `DATE` key column. Each label must receive the latest snapshot on or before its own date. What is the fix?

choices.text: Change `snap_date` to `STRING`, which keeps all the history and makes each lookup return the most recent earlier snapshot for the label
Remove `snap_date` from the key and overwrite the table every night, so that each label is joined to the single newest row of its customer
Upgrade `databricks-feature-engineering`, because newer releases treat any `DATE` key column as a time series column without a declaration
Declare `snap_date` as the `TIMESERIES` key column of the table and set `timestamp_lookup_key` on the `FeatureLookup` to the label's date column

stem: A time series feature table for ad impressions has key `(region, advertiser_id, campaign_id, ts TIMESERIES)` and 6 billion rows. Writes and training-set lookups are slower than expected. Which redesign follows Databricks guidance for performant writes and lookups?

choices.text: Merge the three entity columns into one entity key column and keep `(campaign_key, ts TIMESERIES)` as a two-column key with liquid clustering
Declare `campaign_id` as a second `TIMESERIES` column so that the as-of join can also match the campaign by recency
Partition the table by `region` and by `ts` so that every as-of lookup reads only the partition that matches its label timestamp
Move `ts` out of the key into an ordinary feature column, so that lookups need only the entity columns and run as exact matches

stem: A Lakeflow Job task writes hourly rows to the time series table `ml.ops.store_hourly` (key `(store_id, hour_ts TIMESERIES)`) with `fe.write_table(name=..., df=hour_df, mode="merge")`. After a transient failure the task is retried and re-writes hours that were already stored. What happens, and what must stay true?

choices.text: Rows already stored are skipped and keep their old values, so corrected values from the retry never reach the table
Rows are appended a second time, since a time series table is append-only, so the job needs an extra step that removes the duplicates
Rows with the same `(store_id, hour_ts)` are matched and updated, so the retry is safe while each row still carries every feature
The retry fails on the first repeated row with a key violation, so the job must delete the stored hours before it runs again

stem: A platform team wants to expose the view `ml.crm.v_cust_orders`, defined as `SELECT c.id, SUM(o.amt) spend FROM customers c JOIN orders o USING(id) GROUP BY c.id`, as a feature table. Registering it fails. What is the correct approach?

choices.text: Add a `PRIMARY KEY (id)` constraint directly on the view, then reuse it in `create_training_set` with no change to its definition
Wrap the view in a SQL UDF and pass it as a `FeatureFunction` so the aggregation runs on every lookup of the table
Upgrade `databricks-feature-engineering` to a newer release, because every Unity Catalog view with a key column is accepted from that version onward
Compute the aggregation into a Delta table with a primary key on `id` in a scheduled job, and use that table; only simple SELECT views qualify

stem: Training rows have `user_id`, `ad_id`, `session_start_ts` and `impression_ts`. User features (time series table) must be as of the session start; ad features (another time series table) as of the impression. How should the training set be built?

choices.text: Put both timestamp columns into the primary key of each feature table and join on the composite key in the label DataFrame
Define one `FeatureLookup` per table, each with its own `timestamp_lookup_key`, and pass both to a single `create_training_set` call
Choose one `timestamp_lookup_key` for the whole call and shift the other timestamp in the source data so that both tables agree
Create two training sets, one per feature table with its own timestamp, then union the outputs and drop the duplicate label rows

stem: A feature table with 40 million customers is recomputed every night and about 80% of the rows change. The online store must reflect the new values by morning, and no updates arrive during the day. Which publish mode is the best fit?

choices.text: `CONTINUOUS`, which keeps a streaming pipeline running all day to apply each source change to the online store as it happens
`CONTINUOUS` for the first week, then `TRIGGERED`, because the mode can be switched in place once enough data has been loaded
`SNAPSHOT`, which copies all data from the source table in one sync and suits runs where many existing rows change between syncs
`TRIGGERED`, because incremental sync is always faster than a full copy, even when most rows change between two runs

stem: Two Lakeflow Job tasks, each ending with `fe.publish_table(online_store=store, source_table_name="ml.crm.cust_features", online_table_name="ml.crm.cust_features_online")`, sometimes log: "Skipping publishing to online table ... because the feature sync pipeline is already running." What is the recommended design?

choices.text: Create a second online table for the second task so that each notebook has its own sync pipeline to write into without waiting
Add `time.sleep(600)` to the second task so the first has finished, and retry the publish call in a loop up to three times
Switch the table to `SNAPSHOT` mode, which allows several simultaneous syncs because it only copies the data once per run
Publish from one place, such as a single final task, or wait with `get_status()` for the running sync before calling again

stem: A production online feature store runs without high availability. The team now needs HA, and disabling or changing it on the live store would disconnect Feature Serving and Model Serving endpoints that read from it. How should they change the configuration with the least disruption?

choices.text: Delete only the published online tables, change the store setting, then run `publish_table` again so the same tables return to service
Create a new store with the target settings, publish the tables, point new endpoints at it, validate, then retire the old endpoints and store
Change the setting on the live store in a maintenance window, then wait for the connected endpoints to reconnect without any manual action
Put a second endpoint on the same store with a larger workload size so requests can fail over to it while the setting is changed

stem: To cut cost, an engineer drops an unused online table with `DROP TABLE ml.crm.cust_features_online` and sees no savings on the Lakebase side. Which statement is correct and what should be done?

choices.text: Use the SDK method `delete_online_table`, which removes the table from Unity Catalog and the database; a SQL drop leaves the data in place
Delete the source offline feature table, because the online table is removed when the table that it was published from disappears
Dropping with SQL is correct, and the savings appear after the next sync cycle clears the database pages that the table had used
Set the store to scale to zero, which releases the stored data of every unused online table while the store itself stays available

stem: A team deleted and recreated the online table `ml.crm.cust_features_online` (same name) under a live Feature Serving endpoint. The endpoint reports Ready and the sync pipeline succeeds, but lookups fail with "password authentication failed". What is the cause and recovery?

choices.text: The new table is a new securable and the endpoint lost its `SELECT` grant; serving a new `FeatureSpec` rebuilds the endpoint
The sync pipeline stopped, so run `publish_table` again until the status reaches `AVAILABLE` and the endpoint recovers by itself without changes
The endpoint cache is stale, so stopping and starting the endpoint, or redeploying it unchanged, rebuilds it and re-resolves the table
The online store password expired, so rotate the Lakebase credentials in the store settings and keep the same endpoint configuration

stem: A feature table was published to a second online table in a new store during a migration. Weeks later, the Model Serving endpoint still returns values that match the old store, not the new one. Why?

choices.text: The new store is still replicating, so the endpoint will switch over by itself once the first full sync has completed without any errors
The endpoint resolves to the oldest online table of that feature table, so migrate with a new feature table version to move traffic
The endpoint keeps a fixed copy of the feature values taken at deployment, so only redeploying with a larger workload size reloads the values
Endpoints always read from the newest online table, so the new table must be failing silently and its sync pipeline must be restarted

stem: A fraud model needs per-card velocity features updated within seconds of a transaction, served by Model Serving with automatic lookup, and reproducible for training. The events arrive on a streaming source. Which design satisfies all three needs?

choices.text: Use a scheduled `TRIGGERED` publish every minute from a notebook that recomputes the velocity features for all cards over their full history
Compute velocity on demand from the raw transaction list that the caller sends in each request, and skip stored features entirely
Stream events into the offline table with `write_table(mode="merge")` and publish it `CONTINUOUS`, with Change Data Feed enabled
Write the streaming results directly into Lakebase tables and have the endpoint query them by hand with custom code inside the model

stem: A fraud model needs `txn_count_10min` per card and `amount_ratio` (current amount divided by the card's 30-day average). Cards produce thousands of events per second. Which split is best?

choices.text: Precompute both in the stream and store them in a feature table, since a stored feature is always faster than a function evaluated per request
Compute both on demand in a Unity Catalog Python function at request time, using the raw event history of the card as an input to the function
Compute both in a nightly batch job and publish them online, because the model only needs daily freshness for fraud decisions
Stream `txn_count_10min` and the 30-day average into a feature table with a watermark, and compute `amount_ratio` on demand from the request

stem: A stream upserts the latest `last_login_ts` per user into a plain feature table (key `user_id`) through `write_table(mode="merge")`. Late-arriving events overwrite newer values with older ones. Which change handles out-of-order data best?

choices.text: Sort the stream by arrival time with `orderBy` before the merge so that the last arrival is always the newest event
Add `event_ts` as an ordinary column and trust the merge to keep whichever row has the higher value in that column
Key a time series table `(user_id, event_ts TIMESERIES)`, so each event is its own row and lookups return the latest row by event time
Increase the stream trigger interval so that late events always arrive before the micro-batch is processed and merged into the table

stem: Peak traffic raises p99 latency of feature lookups from an online feature store (created with `create_online_store`), while the streaming writes keep up. CPU on the primary is saturated by reads. What is the best response?

choices.text: Publish the same feature table to a second online table in the store so that endpoints share read traffic between both tables
Add read replicas with `read_replica_count` (up to three) and, if needed, more capacity, so read traffic is spread
Increase the shuffle partitions of the streaming query so that writes finish faster and free up resources on the online store
Switch the publish mode to `SNAPSHOT` to reduce the number of small incremental writes that compete with reads on the primary

stem: A source delivers transactions at least once, so the same `txn_id` can appear twice within minutes. A streaming job computes `txn_count_10min` per card, which is inflated. Which fix bounds state while removing duplicates before aggregation?

choices.text: Apply `withWatermark("event_ts", "10 minutes")` and `dropDuplicates(["txn_id", "event_ts"])` before the windowed count
Replace `merge` with `append` in `write_table`, since appended rows are deduplicated by primary key when the table is read
Call `distinct()` on the stream in each micro-batch so that the repeated events from the previous batches are also removed
Deduplicate after the aggregation by dividing the count by the average number of repeats observed in a sample

stem: A pricing model needs `bid_ratio = request_bid / avg_bid_30d`. The 30-day average is a stored feature; `request_bid` exists only in the request. The ratio must be computed identically in training, batch scoring and Model Serving. What is the best implementation?

choices.text: Compute `bid_ratio` in the training notebook with pandas, and ask client applications to compute the same ratio before they call the endpoint
Store `bid_ratio` in the feature table and refresh it hourly, so the endpoint can look up the ratio like any other feature
Add the ratio logic inside a custom pyfunc and keep training on columns that were computed separately in a notebook
Register a Python UDF in Unity Catalog, bind it with a `FeatureFunction`, and log the model with `fe.log_model(..., training_set=training_set)`

stem: An on-demand UDF takes `x`, a value from a `FeatureLookup`, and returns `x * x`. Batch scoring works. For brand-new users, the online endpoint returns errors, though the same users score in batch. What is the likely cause and fix?

choices.text: Online serving requires scalar UDFs to be written in SQL, so rewrite the function as a SQL expression without any Python
The online store rejects new users, so rerun `publish_table` in `SNAPSHOT` mode until the new users appear in the table
Missing lookups reach the UDF as `None` in `score_batch` but as `float("nan")` online, so the function must handle both cases
Python UDFs cannot read values from `FeatureLookup`, so pass the lookup value in the request payload as a raw input

stem: An on-demand UDF imports `scipy` for a statistic. The model trains and scores in a notebook, but the Model Serving deployment fails during the build. What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Install `scipy` on the cluster used for training as a cluster library, which Model Serving copies into the endpoint at deployment
Add `import scipy` to the top of the Unity Catalog function, because the serving image installs imported modules at startup
Remove the import and send precomputed statistics from the client, since UDFs may only use the Python standard library
Declare the package with `extra_pip_requirements` in `fe.log_model`, or when creating the FeatureSpec for Feature Serving

stem: A rules engine (not an ML model) needs `spending_gap = ytd_spend - average_yearly_spend` for a user on every call, where `ytd_spend` comes from the caller and the average from a feature table. A data scientist suggests deploying a dummy model. What is the better design?

choices.text: Create a `FeatureSpec` with a lookup and a function, publish the table online, and serve it through a Feature Serving endpoint
Create the feature table as a view and let the rules engine compute the gap in its own application code on every call
Query the offline Delta table through a SQL warehouse on every call, because Feature Serving endpoints cannot read online tables
Deploy a dummy model that returns its input unchanged, because only Model Serving endpoints can host Unity Catalog UDFs

stem: A model was trained with features that are looked up from an online store. For one request, the caller already has a fresher value of a stored feature, `cart_value`, from its own session. How can the caller use it without changing the model?

choices.text: Send the value in a custom HTTP header, which Model Serving maps onto the stored feature by name automatically
Include the feature value in the request payload; it overrides the looked-up value and must match the data type the model expects
Write the value into the feature table, publish it in `CONTINUOUS` mode, and send the request after the sync finishes
Retrain the model with `cart_value` as an on-demand feature so that the caller can send it in the request in future releases
